text: A private camera caught a public killing, and everything since has been an argument about what its frames can be made to show. Abraham Zapruder's home footage is the whole source of this film, and H.D. Motyl gives it eighty-eight minutes: cleaned, steadied, enlarged, run again. The proportion is the point. Amateur stock was never meant to bear that kind of attention, and the re-mastering both improves the image and makes plain where improvement stops. What results is a documentary about the examination of a document rather than about the event, a stranger and more patient thing than the subject suggests. The National Film Registry keeps it. Whatever one believes about the killing, the narrower question here is how much can be asked of a picture before it stops answering.

Norteno music is working music, made for people who have to be up in the morning. Les Blank filmed its players along the Texas-Mexican border, and the fifty-eight minutes he brought back give as much room to the lives around the songs as to the songs themselves. Flaco Jimenez plays. So does Lydia Mendoza. The film takes music and labor as one subject, which is why the Chicano experience it records comes through detail rather than argument: who is in the room, who is listening, what gets said between numbers. Some editions carry Del Mero Corazon alongside it. A border is usually filmed as a line; here it is a place where particular people live and play, and the camera stays close enough to register the difference.

Thirty-five hostages, one prison yard, and a list of demands that men had already tried making the quiet way. Cinda Firestone's film returns to the 1971 days when inmates held D-yard at Attica State Prison, and it works less like reportage than like an audit: what was said at the time set against what was said afterward, and both against the record. Eighty minutes, and nothing in the pacing offers comfort. The uprising itself takes up less room than the machinery around it — who authorized, who testified, how far the two accounts drift apart. Only three years separate the film from the yard, close enough that the language of officials had not yet been tidied into history, and close enough that the men speaking are speaking about something recent.

Two strangers agree to track down a runaway waitress for the reward money, and then, having found her, decide against collecting it. What follows is the film: three people walking, one of them heading for a town called Sampo that he left ten years ago. Lee Man-hee gives them a hundred and one minutes and very little incident. The young man has come through a jail and a construction site; the older one carries a place in his head; the woman has walked out of the restaurant that employed her. They are the sort of labor that follows building work around the country, and their talk does what plot does elsewhere. It is a road film whose destination exists mainly as one man's decade-old memory of it, and the walking is not a delay before the meaning arrives.

A tape company ran a contest, the Barstow family won it, and the prize was a week in California at a park that had only just opened. Robbins and Meg Barstow brought their own camera. Thirty-five minutes came back, and they keep what a professional crew would cut: the packing, the travelling, the small ceremonies of a family on a trip it never planned. Disneyland was new then, new to everyone photographing it, and nobody in the frame has yet learned how such a place is supposed to be enjoyed. The amateurism is the value. No one is composing for posterity, so the camera follows the family rather than the attractions, and the record it leaves is of an ordinary household briefly inside an advertisement. The National Film Registry took it in, which is a strange fate for a home movie about winning a prize.

Steel arrives at one end of a Chevrolet plant and a car is driven off the other; the film lives entirely in the distance between those two facts. Thirty-three minutes, the middle of the 1930s, and the material is process — metal formed, parts joined, bodies finished, each operation handed on to the next. What holds attention now is not the engineering but the workers standing inside it. Cars were built then by people positioned very close to very large machines, at the speed the machines set, and a camera was allowed onto the floor while that was going on. A finished automobile is designed to hide its own making. Thirty-three minutes of the making is a correction, and the shape of the film is supplied by the plant rather than by any story.

Someone pointed a camera at a march through Cicero and cut the result down to eight minutes. It is numbered — module seven of a series called The Urban Crisis and the New Militants — which means it was made for rooms where a discussion would follow, and the discussion is not in the film. Mike Gray shot it in 1966. Eight minutes leaves no space for context, interviews or summary; what fits is a street, a column of people moving along it, and whoever else happens to be there. The constraint is why it still works. Accounts of the period written later arrive with the argument already assembled; this arrives as a duration, the length of time it takes to walk a few blocks in a place where the walking was itself the argument.

A boy has been left at a Buddhist temple, and the day there has a shape that will not bend to accommodate him. Meals, chores, hours kept by other people's discipline; the adults around him are bound by rule rather than blood. Then a young widow arrives to mourn a son who has died. Yoon Yong-gyu's film, made in 1949 and running seventy-seven minutes, lets the attachment between them form in glances and small errands instead of declarations, which is also the only way it could form in such a place. The setting supplies the tenderness and the impediment at once, since a temple is organized around giving things up. Two people need the same thing from opposite directions. The film is careful never to say so out loud.

The man at the centre is a reporter, filing for a North Korean news service, until he sets the job down and joins the partisans. The reversal gives Chung Ji-young's film its vantage: someone trained to watch and describe, placed inside an irregular war that will not let him keep any distance from it. Two hours and thirty-seven minutes. The length is a decision about texture rather than scope, a war measured in marches, waiting and weather rather than in named battles. What makes the film unusual is where it was made — South Korea, 1990 — with its central figure on the northern side and the story told from within his unit. The camera stays with that unit, so the war arrives only at the speed the men in it learn of anything.

An intertitle sets out the local law before the story does: man is absolute ruler, woman is working slave. What follows tests that sentence against a country boy who has picked up an idea of chivalry somewhere outside his father's house and cannot make it fit inside it. Karl Brown's 1927 film runs seventy minutes, and its subject is a household in which the division of labor and the division of authority are the same division. The boy's wish to get out, and to take the girl he loves with him, is less a romance than a proposition about who is permitted to decide anything. Silent melodrama usually borrows its cruelty from villains. Here the cruelty is a domestic arrangement, stated plainly on a title card and then simply allowed to operate.

The horse and cart still work; it is the city that has stopped needing them. A man makes his living driving one through a Korea rebuilding itself out of what the war left, and the automobiles make his trade a little more ornamental every year. Kang Dae-jin spends much of the ninety-eight minutes on the man's four children, each attached to a different exit: an eldest son who has failed the bar examination twice, a daughter married into a violent house, another daughter passing herself off as a wealthy student, a youngest boy already stealing. The family drama is entirely economic. It holds together on the father's daily route, which brings in exactly what it brings in, and on the examination, which is the one future anyone in the house can name out loud.

Wages set this story moving: a woman named Oh takes a job at a boutique to help make a living, and from behind that counter the rest of the city looks different. Han Hyeong-mo spends a hundred and twenty-five minutes on what follows, and a good deal of it goes to the adults arranged around her — Professor Jang, the typist Miss Park — whose attachments form and come apart in workplaces rather than in parlours. This is 1956 melodrama in which earning is the engine of everything else, and feeling gets negotiated through employment, correspondence and reputation while the film keeps its voice level. A shop counter is a small stage. The drama begins with the plain fact that a woman now has somewhere else to be during the day.

A fourteen-minute film made in 1920 exists to tell immigrants that English is the price of getting on. Guy Hedlund built the lesson out of the equipment of drama — characters, a difficulty, an improvement — so that the argument would go down as a story rather than as a lecture. The persuasion is not concealed, because at the time there was no reason to conceal it, and that candour is what makes it worth looking at now: the film states what the country wanted from the people arriving, and how quickly. Later arguments about assimilation are conducted in careful language. This one is conducted in a plot, which makes the shape of the demand plain — what was to be given up, in what order, and what was offered in return.

The performance was staged for the camera, and the film says as much; that admission is where its interest begins. Gregory Bateson shot the Kris Dance in Bali in 1937, and the twenty-two minutes were not released until 1952. The footage is organized to record rather than to dramatize — placement chosen so that movement stays legible, trance and possession approached as events occurring in particular bodies at particular moments rather than as spectacle to be built. Two documents therefore sit inside one reel. The first is a ritual, danced. The second is the arrangement that produced the first: a ceremony performed because an outsider with equipment asked for it, on terms the film does not disguise. Watching one without the other is possible, and it is the poorer way to spend the twenty-two minutes.
